title: RNA World
author: Philip Ball
dek: A single polymer that stores the recipe and runs the kitchen — before DNA, before proteins.

sections.heading: One molecule, two jobs
sections.body:
PLACEHOLDER — full paragraph(s) go here verbatim from doc.

The RNA World is the most famous first chapter in origins research. It says life began as a polymer that could both carry information and catalyze reactions — a {ribozyme|An RNA molecule capable of catalyzing chemical reactions.} that copies itself, or copies a cousin, before DNA or coded proteins exist.

The attraction is economy. You do not need a translation system yet. You do not need a genome written in a more stable alphabet. You need a strand, a way to concentrate it, and enough time for Darwinian copying to begin.

sections.speaker: Walter Gilbert
sections.text: The first stage of evolution proceeded by RNA molecules performing the catalytic activities necessary to assemble themselves from a nucleotide soup.

sections.heading: What the story still owes us
sections.body:
PLACEHOLDER — full paragraph(s) go here verbatim from doc.

Making RNA from a lifeless Earth is not a solved problem. Nucleotides are fussy. Water attacks polymers. A replicating ribozyme in a dilute pond is a hope, not a demonstration.

This piece holds the RNA World still: its elegance, its experimental near-misses, and the reasons some researchers think it is a beautiful second chapter pretending to be the first.
